The Greek company PPC, the leading South-East European integrated utility Group, will acquire the two companies, including all 38 ABO Energy employees in the two countries, a development pipeline with a total capacity of around two gigawatts, and five operational solar parks with a combined capacity of 82 megawatts as well as a 17 megawatts solar farm nearing completion. The sale will have no impact on the development of ABO Energy’s planned restructuring and financing solution. 'Following the sale of our Greek subsidiary and most of our Finnish wind power pipeline, the sale of our Hungarian and Polish subsidiaries marks another step towards focusing on those countries where we can achieve sustainable long-term commercial success,' said Managing Director Dr Karsten Schlageter . 'We are pleased to have found a good solution both for ABO Energy and for the employees concerned.' Subject to the necessary regulatory approvals, closing of the transaction is expected by the end of the year. ABO Energy has been active as a project developer in Poland and Hungary since 2019. During this time, the company has developed and sold renewable energy projects in both countries while building a substantial development pipeline. ABO Energy’s objective remains unchanged: to agree a sustainable restructuring and financing solution for the company in the coming weeks and months. http://eng.chinamil.com.cn/2025xb/W/N/16.text: China Military HOME CHINA Featured Story Training & Exercise Exchange & Cooperation Military Operations Other Than War Law Enforcement VOICE OPINION WORLD World News Analysis MULTIMEDIA Photo Video Lithuania eyes permanent US military base, Russia warns of escalation A Russian Navy strike group conducting combat drills in the Baltic Sea, June 23, 2025. /VCG Lithuania said on Tuesday that it stands ready to cover the costs of hosting a permanent US military base, while Russia said that any deployment of NATO infrastructure or nuclear weapons on Lithuanian soil would further escalate regional tensions. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said on Tuesday that Lithuania is ready to pay the cost to set up a permanent US military base if Washington should âagree to establish one there, a day after US President Donald Trump said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent base. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, on the same day, said that the possible deployment of a NATO military base and nuclear weapons in Lithuania would further escalate tensions. "Both of these things will not contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will become another significant round in the escalation of tensions," Peskov said. Peskov added that if such deployment occurs, Russia would be forced to take retaliatory measures to ensure its national security. A constitutional amendment to lift a ban on weapons of mass destruction, potentially opening the way for stationing NATO nuclear weapons in Lithuania, passed the first reading in the Lithuanian parliament earlier on Tuesday. A final vote on the amendment has been scheduled for January 12, 2027. Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border with Russia's exclave of Kaliningrad. The United States has kept an armored battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning âthe troops arrive and leave every few months. Sinkevicius said he proposed turning this into a permanent presence at a meeting with Trump's envoy John Coale last month in Vilnius. The latest development comes as Russia recently issued a warning over NATO's military activities in the Baltic region, saying it is prepared to use all means at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO attempts to blockade Russia's Kaliningrad region. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte responded last week by describing NATO as a "defensive alliance" and condemning what he called Russia's "nuclear threats." Moscow said it poses no threat to anyone. The exchange has remained largely rhetorical, but highlights rising tensions around Kaliningrad and the broader Baltic region. The recent tensions in the Baltic appear to be directly linked to repeated drone disputes between Russia and Baltic coastal states, while NATO has increasingly pressured Russia by targeting its socioeconomic stability, said Chen Yu, deputy director of the Institute of Eurasian Studies at the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations. More fundamentally, Chen said, this is the inevitable result of a shift in NATO's Baltic strategy: after the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict since February 2022, NATO's presence in the Baltic has gradually upgraded from rotational deterrence to permanent basing, pushing military pressure right up to Russia's border. Chen said the Baltic states hope to use nuclear deterrence to offset Russia's military power, driven by rising security anxiety and a desire to align with US strategic agenda, as Washington actively discusses expanding its nuclear deployment plans in Europe. In response, he said, Russia is likely to further strengthen its nuclear forces in Kaliningrad, deploy more tactical nuclear weapons and hypersonic weapons, and enhance the nuclear-conventional strike capability of its Baltic Fleet so as to defend its red lines while avoiding being cornered into a full confrontation. https://www.wkms.org/npr-news/2026-11-06.text: On Air Now Playing WKMS On Air Now Playing WKMS Music On Air Now Playing WKMS Classical NPR News Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank NPR | By Jenna McLaughlin Published November 6, 2026 at 1:00 PM CST Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Helene Rigny / Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images A close up of the hands of a nurse from the French Blood Establishment checking the identification and traceability of blood samples beside a donor during a mobile blood donation session in Paimpol Cotes d Armor Brittany France on July 23, 2026. In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank. "This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps. Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage. However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable. "This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life." On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation. The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk." "Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said. Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples. It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups. Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit. Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims. Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. "Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR. "It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued. Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways. For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure. Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss. While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there. Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model. Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks. Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign. "Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse." Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents. The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy. Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks. That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms." In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency. Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems. Store managers on the frontlines Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster. While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact." Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves. "The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote. "Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."
